title: Mental Health — EPS & NMS II: Differentiation, Priority & Emergency Response (Set 25)
subtitle: Phase-2 depth: telling the extrapyramidal symptoms apart and matching the response (acute dystonia emergency vs akathisia vs pseudoparkinsonism fall risk vs tardive dyskinesia), distinguishing neuroleptic malignant syndrome from serotonin syndrome and from simple infection, prioritizing the deteriorating client, supportive NMS care and dose-hold/report, anticholinergic-treatment cautions, early recognition and teaching, and the technician's monitoring/reporting role
scenario: Catching medication emergencies early: recognizing acute dystonia and NMS as emergencies, telling akathisia from anxiety and NMS from serotonin syndrome, protecting the client from falls and injury, and reporting so licensed staff can act.

steps.q: A client on a first-generation antipsychotic suddenly develops a severe, sustained neck spasm with the head twisted to one side. The technician recognizes acute dystonia and should FIRST:

opts.text: Stay with the client, ensure the airway is not compromised, and notify the nurse immediately, anticipating an ordered anticholinergic
opts.rat: Acute dystonia is distressing and can involve the throat muscles, so airway safety and prompt reporting come first, anticipating an ordered anticholinergic (e.g., benztropine or diphenhydramine).

opts.text: Tell the client to relax and check back in an hour
opts.rat: Acute dystonia is an emergency needing prompt intervention, not delayed reassessment.

opts.text: Give the next scheduled antipsychotic dose early
opts.rat: More antipsychotic can worsen the reaction; it is not the response.

opts.text: Document it as normal and take no further action
opts.rat: Acute dystonia is reported and treated, not ignored.

steps.q: Why is it important to distinguish akathisia (drug-induced inner restlessness) from anxiety or worsening agitation?

opts.text: Akathisia is a medication side effect; treating it as agitation by increasing the antipsychotic can make it worse—so it is reported for the team to address
opts.rat: Mistaking akathisia for agitation and raising the antipsychotic dose can worsen it; correct recognition and reporting lead to appropriate management.

opts.text: There is no difference, so no distinction is needed
opts.rat: The distinction changes management, so it matters.

opts.text: Akathisia should always be treated with more of the same antipsychotic
opts.rat: Increasing the causative drug can worsen akathisia.

opts.text: Akathisia never needs to be reported
opts.rat: Akathisia is distressing and is reported so it can be managed.

steps.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops a shuffling gait, stiffness, and a mask-like face (drug-induced parkinsonism). Regarding safety, the technician should PRIORITIZE:

opts.text: Fall and injury precautions and assistance with movement, and report the findings
opts.rat: Rigidity, bradykinesia, and a shuffling gait raise fall risk, so assistance and precautions protect the client while the findings are reported.

opts.text: Encouraging the client to walk fast without help to loosen up
opts.rat: Fast unassisted walking is unsafe for a stiff, bradykinetic client.

opts.text: Assuming the gait is laziness and ignoring it
opts.rat: This is a medication effect, not laziness, and it is reported.

opts.text: Restricting all movement indefinitely
opts.rat: The client needs safe assisted mobility and precautions, not blanket restriction.

steps.q: A client on long-term antipsychotics develops involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements (tardive dyskinesia). A key point for the technician is that:

opts.text: Tardive dyskinesia can be persistent or irreversible, so early recognition and reporting are important
opts.rat: Because tardive dyskinesia may not fully reverse, catching and reporting early involuntary movements matters so the team can respond.

opts.text: It always resolves quickly on its own with no reporting needed
opts.rat: Tardive dyskinesia can be lasting; it is reported, not dismissed.

opts.text: It is treated by giving extra doses of the same antipsychotic
opts.rat: Extra antipsychotic does not treat tardive dyskinesia and can contribute to it.

opts.text: It is the same emergency as acute dystonia
opts.rat: Tardive dyskinesia is a chronic movement disorder, not the acute airway-threatening emergency dystonia can be.

steps.q: Among these clients, who is the technician's PRIORITY to assess and report first?

opts.text: A client on an antipsychotic with a high fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, and unstable vital signs
opts.rat: Fever, 'lead-pipe' rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome—a medical emergency and the top priority.

opts.text: A client with a mild dry mouth from an anticholinergic
opts.rat: Dry mouth is a minor side effect, not an emergency.

opts.text: A client asking about the lunch menu
opts.rat: A routine question is not a priority over a possible NMS emergency.

opts.text: A stable client attending group
opts.rat: A stable client is not the acute priority.

steps.q: When neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is suspected, the appropriate immediate response is to:

opts.text: Hold the antipsychotic, notify the nurse/provider urgently, and support cooling, hydration, and close vital-sign monitoring as ordered
opts.rat: NMS is an emergency: the causative drug is held, help is summoned urgently, and supportive measures (cooling, hydration, monitoring) are provided per orders.

opts.text: Give another dose of the antipsychotic to calm the client
opts.rat: Continuing the causative drug worsens NMS.

opts.text: Wait until the next shift to mention it
opts.rat: NMS requires urgent action, not delay.

opts.text: Encourage the client to exercise to bring the fever down
opts.rat: Exertion is unsafe in an unstable, rigid, febrile client.

steps.q: Both NMS and serotonin syndrome can cause fever and altered mental status. A feature that points more toward serotonin syndrome is:

opts.text: Overactive reflexes and muscle twitching (hyperreflexia/clonus) after a serotonergic medication
opts.rat: Serotonin syndrome typically features hyperreflexia and clonus and follows serotonergic drugs, whereas NMS features 'lead-pipe' rigidity after antipsychotics.

opts.text: Slow, 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity after starting an antipsychotic
opts.rat: Lead-pipe rigidity after an antipsychotic points toward NMS.

opts.text: Onset only after years of stable antipsychotic use
opts.rat: This timing does not distinguish serotonin syndrome; it commonly follows serotonergic drug changes.

opts.text: The complete absence of any autonomic changes
opts.rat: Both syndromes involve autonomic changes, so this does not distinguish them.

steps.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops a fever. The technician should:

opts.text: Consider NMS as a possibility—checking for rigidity, confusion, and unstable vital signs—and report promptly rather than assuming it is only a routine infection
opts.rat: A fever in a client on antipsychotics warrants a high index of suspicion for NMS; associated rigidity and instability are assessed and reported promptly.

opts.text: Assume it is always a minor cold and take no action
opts.rat: Assuming a minor cause can miss NMS; the possibility is evaluated and reported.

opts.text: Give the next antipsychotic dose and recheck tomorrow
opts.rat: If NMS is developing, continuing the drug is dangerous; prompt reporting is needed.

opts.text: Ignore the fever unless the client complains loudly
opts.rat: A fever on antipsychotics is significant and is reported.

steps.q: Which extrapyramidal problem is the ACUTE emergency requiring the most immediate response?

opts.text: Acute dystonia, especially if it involves the muscles of the throat and threatens the airway
opts.rat: Acute dystonia can involve the laryngeal muscles and compromise the airway, making it the acute EPS emergency.

opts.text: Long-standing tardive dyskinesia
opts.rat: Tardive dyskinesia is a chronic problem, not an acute airway emergency.

opts.text: Mild, stable drug-induced tremor
opts.rat: A mild stable tremor is reported but is not the acute emergency.

opts.text: Slowly progressing mask-like facial expression
opts.rat: This parkinsonian sign is monitored and reported but is not the acute airway emergency.

steps.q: Anticholinergic medications (such as benztropine) are sometimes ordered to manage EPS. The technician should monitor for their own side effects, which include:

opts.text: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion (especially in older adults)
opts.rat: Anticholinergics used for EPS commonly cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion, particularly in the elderly.

opts.text: Increased salivation and diarrhea
opts.rat: Anticholinergics reduce secretions and slow the gut, not increase salivation/diarrhea.

opts.text: No side effects of any kind
opts.rat: These medications have notable anticholinergic side effects to monitor.

opts.text: Improved memory and alertness in older adults
opts.rat: Anticholinergics can worsen confusion in older adults, not improve cognition.

steps.q: A withdrawn client on an antipsychotic cannot clearly describe how they feel. To detect EPS, the technician should:

opts.text: Observe objectively for abnormal movements, rigidity, restlessness, gait changes, and facial expression, and report findings
opts.rat: Because EPS can be observed, careful objective monitoring of movement, tone, restlessness, and gait detects problems even when the client cannot verbalize them.

opts.text: Assume there is no problem because the client did not complain
opts.rat: EPS can be present without the client reporting it; observation is needed.

opts.text: Wait for the client to file a formal complaint
opts.rat: Detection relies on observation, not on the client complaining.

opts.text: Only check if a family member raises a concern
opts.rat: Routine objective monitoring is the technician's responsibility.

steps.q: A client experiencing akathisia is visibly distressed and says they 'can't stand feeling like this.' The technician should recognize that:

opts.text: Akathisia is very distressing and has been linked to increased agitation and distress, so it is reported promptly for management and the client's safety is monitored
opts.rat: Severe akathisia is highly distressing and can heighten agitation and distress, so prompt reporting and safety monitoring are appropriate.

opts.text: Akathisia is trivial and the complaint can be dismissed
opts.rat: Akathisia is genuinely distressing and is taken seriously.

opts.text: The client is simply seeking attention
opts.rat: This is a real medication effect, not attention-seeking.

opts.text: It requires no reporting or follow-up
opts.rat: Distressing akathisia is reported so it can be managed.

steps.q: A client recovering from NMS asks when they can restart their antipsychotic. The technician should:

opts.text: Explain that any decision to resume or change antipsychotics is made cautiously by the provider, and relay the question to the team
opts.rat: Restarting an antipsychotic after NMS is a careful prescriber decision; the technician refers the question rather than advising on it.

opts.text: Tell the client to resume the same dose right away
opts.rat: Advising resumption is outside scope and unsafe after NMS.

opts.text: Say they can never take any psychiatric medication again
opts.rat: This is inaccurate and outside scope; the provider evaluates options.

opts.text: Tell the client to decide on their own
opts.rat: Medication decisions belong to the prescriber, not the client alone or the technician.

steps.q: Which client is generally at HIGHER risk for developing extrapyramidal symptoms, warranting closer monitoring?

opts.text: A client on a high-potency first-generation (typical) antipsychotic
opts.rat: High-potency first-generation antipsychotics are more likely to cause EPS, so these clients are monitored more closely.

opts.text: A client on no psychiatric medication at all
opts.rat: Without an antipsychotic, drug-induced EPS is not the concern.

opts.text: A client taking only a topical skin cream
opts.rat: A topical skin cream is not associated with EPS.

opts.text: A client taking only a daily multivitamin
opts.rat: A multivitamin does not cause EPS.

steps.q: The technician should teach a client and family that which new symptoms after starting an antipsychotic should be reported promptly?

opts.text: Muscle stiffness or spasms, uncontrollable restlessness, abnormal movements, high fever, or confusion
opts.rat: These can signal EPS or NMS and should be reported promptly for evaluation.

opts.text: Feeling calm and sleeping through the night
opts.rat: These are reassuring, not warning signs.

opts.text: A gradual improvement in mood
opts.rat: Mood improvement is a desired effect, not a warning sign.

opts.text: Enjoying meals again
opts.rat: Improved appetite is not a symptom to report as an emergency.

steps.q: While supporting a client with suspected NMS and a high fever, an appropriate supportive nursing measure (as ordered) is to:

opts.text: Assist with cooling measures, support hydration, and monitor vital signs closely while awaiting/carrying out orders
opts.rat: Supportive care for NMS includes cooling, hydration, and close vital-sign monitoring, carried out within scope and per orders.

opts.text: Bundle the client in heavy blankets to raise the temperature
opts.rat: Warming a hyperthermic client is harmful; cooling is indicated.

opts.text: Withhold all fluids
opts.rat: Hydration is part of supportive NMS care, not withheld.

opts.text: Leave the client unmonitored until the provider arrives
opts.rat: An unstable client needs close monitoring, not to be left alone.

steps.q: An older adult client on an antipsychotic is at particular risk from EPS mainly because:

opts.text: Rigidity and gait changes raise fall and injury risk, and older adults can be more sensitive to medication effects
opts.rat: Older adults are more sensitive to medication effects, and EPS-related rigidity and gait changes increase their fall and injury risk.

opts.text: Older adults never develop side effects
opts.rat: Older adults are often more, not less, susceptible to side effects.

opts.text: Age eliminates the need for monitoring
opts.rat: Older adults typically need closer monitoring.

opts.text: EPS only ever occurs in young clients
opts.rat: EPS can occur across ages and is a particular concern in older adults.

steps.q: A client stops taking their antipsychotic, saying, 'The stiffness and restlessness were unbearable.' The MOST therapeutic response is to:

opts.text: Respond nonjudgmentally, acknowledge that the side effects were distressing, and report so the team can address them and discuss options
opts.rat: Side effects are a common reason for nonadherence; a nonjudgmental response plus reporting lets the team manage side effects and preserve treatment.

opts.text: Criticize the client for stopping the medication
opts.rat: Criticism is nontherapeutic and discourages disclosure.

opts.text: Tell the client to just tolerate the side effects silently
opts.rat: Distressing EPS should be reported and managed, not endured silently.

opts.text: Say nothing to the team about the missed doses
opts.rat: Nonadherence and side effects are important to report.

steps.q: Early recognition programs for tardive dyskinesia rely mainly on:

opts.text: Regular, systematic observation for abnormal involuntary movements so changes are caught and reported early
opts.rat: Routine structured movement assessments help detect early tardive dyskinesia so it can be reported before it progresses.

opts.text: Waiting until movements become severe and permanent
opts.rat: Early detection—not waiting for severe movements—is the goal.

opts.text: Increasing the antipsychotic dose at each visit
opts.rat: Routinely increasing the dose is not a screening method and can worsen the problem.

opts.text: Ignoring subtle movements until the client complains
opts.rat: Subtle movements are actively observed, not ignored.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in EPS and NMS is to:

opts.text: Recognize and differentiate the reactions, treat acute dystonia and NMS as emergencies (hold the dose/report per protocol), protect against falls and airway compromise, support the client, and report changes—while medical management belongs to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician recognizes and distinguishes these reactions, escalates the emergencies, protects safety, supports the client, and reports, while diagnosis and medical treatment are the licensed team's responsibility.

opts.text: Independently adjust antipsychotic doses to fix side effects
opts.rat: Dose adjustment is a prescriber decision, outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Ignore side effects as long as the client's mood improves
opts.rat: EPS and NMS are recognized and reported regardless of mood.

opts.text: Assume all fevers and movements are unrelated to medication
opts.rat: A high index of suspicion for medication effects is maintained and reported.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care (antipsychotic extrapyramidal symptoms and neuroleptic malignant syndrome) — Phase-2 depth/application. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level and stated conceptually, marked for faculty confirmation: differentiating the EPS (acute dystonia as an airway-threatening emergency anticipating an ordered anticholinergic such as benztropine/diphenhydramine; akathisia versus anxiety/agitation and why raising the antipsychotic worsens it; drug-induced parkinsonism and its fall risk; tardive dyskinesia as potentially irreversible needing early recognition and systematic movement screening); distinguishing NMS ('lead-pipe' rigidity, fever, altered mentation, autonomic instability after antipsychotics) from serotonin syndrome (hyperreflexia/clonus after serotonergic drugs) and from simple infection; prioritizing the deteriorating client; NMS immediate response (hold the drug, urgent report, supportive cooling/hydration/monitoring as ordered) and cautious provider-led restart; anticholinergic-treatment side effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion—especially in older adults); higher EPS risk with high-potency first-generation antipsychotics; objective observation of nonverbal clients; nonjudgmental handling of side-effect-driven nonadherence; and the technician's recognize/differentiate/escalate/report role with diagnosis and medical management reserved to licensed staff. Specific drug doses, exact temperature or lab cutoffs, and creatine-kinase values are NOT asserted here; base EPS/NMS/serotonin-syndrome recognition and drug specifics are introduced in mh-core-06. Builds on and does not duplicate mh-core-06. Pending faculty review.
